tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark code is public (src/benchmarks/benchmarks.cpp, std::find in src/cpp_stl/cpp_stl_find.cpp) and the README table compares against std::find on a raw array and on std::vector, but no CPU model is stated, the compiler used for the table is not named (CMakeLists.txt has separate GCC and Clang flag sets) and the README figures are rounded with no raw output for the std::find rows, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (4096 int elements, target in the last slot, G-elements/s, rounded): std::find on a raw array ~7.7 and on std::vector ~8.1 vs FIND_IntrinsicFind (AVX2 cmpeq + movemask, 2x unrolled) ~24.9, about 3.2x over raw-array std::find (derived from page data), and FIND_IntrinsicFloatFind ~25.3; naive loop ~4.6. FIND_Intrinsic2Find ~49.7 is not a find: it counts elements below the target over the whole array (lower_bound on sorted input) and its final reduction is wrong, so it is not a valid speedup over std::find.
corrections.caveats: Personal experiment with no licence file and no hardware stated. The archived docs/perf_results/results.txt is an older run (BM_ names, no CPU header; perf stat files show 24 CPUs only) that has no std::find or Intrinsic2 rows and gives IntrinsicFind/4096 at 21.06 G/s and NaiveFind/4096 at 4.48 G/s, lower than the README's ~24.9; the README's std::find numbers have no raw output in the repo. intrinsic2_find (src/intrinsics/intrinsic_find.cpp) counts elements less than the target with no early exit (a lower_bound on sorted input, not std::find semantics) and its reduction returns _mm256_extract_epi32(sum,0)+_mm256_extract_epi32(sum,1), which is twice the sum of lanes 0-3 and ignores the upper 128-bit half; on the benchmark input (4095 zeros then the target) it returns 4096 instead of 4095. intrinsic_find has no tail loop: it always reads 16 elements per step, so sizes that are not a multiple of 16 read past the buffer (the benchmark rounds sizes 2 and 4 up to 8 and then reads 8 ints beyond the malloc). Both sides are compiled with -Ofast -march=native (GCC) or -O3 -ffast-math (Clang); the std::find side is compiled with the same flags, but which standard library was used is not stated. Numbers are rounded ('~').

notes: Real comparison against std::find; keep at C with the 3.2x IntrinsicFind figure as the claim. New finding: the headline 49.7 G-elements/s Intrinsic2Find row is a different algorithm (full-scan count, lower_bound semantics) whose horizontal reduction is buggy (returns 2x the lanes 0-3 count, 4096 instead of 4095 on the benchmark input), so the 6.5x figure must not be presented as a speedup; intrinsic_find over-reads for sizes not divisible by 16. tier_reason: First-party plots in the README (test/benchmarks/*.png) compare vstat against Boost.Accumulators, GSL, NumPy and linasm on a stated CPU (Ryzen 9 5950X), but no compiler or flags are given, there is no numeric table, and the current benchmark code (TEST_CASE "benchmarks" in test/source/vstat_test.cpp) no longer matches the plotted runs, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Plots only (log-scale op/s vs size, no numeric table); approximate readings at 1M elements, read from the plots, not page text: variance double vstat ~4.4e9 op/s, linasm ~4.4e9 (parity), Boost.Accumulators ~2.5e8 (~17x), NumPy ~1.6e8 (~27x), GSL ~8.5e7 (~50x); variance float vstat ~1.1e10, linasm ~9e9 (~1.2-1.3x), Boost ~2.8e8 (~40x), NumPy ~1.6e8 (~70x), GSL ~8.5e7 (~130x); covariance double vstat ~3.2e9, linasm ~2.3e9 (~1.4x), Boost ~2.3e8 (~14x), GSL ~5.5e7 (~60x), NumPy ~2.9e7 (~110x); covariance float vstat ~6.5e9, linasm ~4.6e9 (~1.4x), Boost ~1.8e8 (~36x), GSL ~5.6e7 (~115x), NumPy ~3e7 (~220x).
corrections.caveats: README gives methodology and CPU but no compiler, flags or numeric table; the four PNG plots are the only results and the figures are approximate readings of log-scale axes. The plots were last committed in November 2021 (Boost 1.69, NumPy 1.19.4 era) and predate the 2026 rewrites of the EVE code; the current benchmark TEST_CASE in test/source/vstat_test.cpp no longer includes NumPy, adds boost.math, uses sizes 1000 to 1M doubling and data in [0,1) rather than the README's 100k steps over [-1,1], so the plots cannot be regenerated from the current code. The presets set no -march flag (Release defaults only), so the SIMD width used for the plots is unknown. vstat ties linasm on double variance and is about 1.2-1.4x faster on the other three plots. MKL was not used for NumPy and GSL (README note); NumPy is measured through Python call overhead; linasm needs precomputed means that were included in its timing; Boost.Accumulators variance is a scalar streaming accumulator. README says C++17 but CMakeLists.txt now requires C++20.

notes: Real first-party comparison against Boost.Accumulators, GSL and NumPy with large ratios; tier C stands (no compiler or flags, stale plots that the current benchmark code does not reproduce). Corrected claimed_speedup to cover all four plots: vstat is not only tied with linasm, it is about 1.2-1.4x ahead except on double variance.
